regulated_activity: Flying/launching a UAS in a state park area

summary: Remote-controlled/unmanned aircraft may be flown in a state park area only within a director-designated flying area under an approved management plan, or under a specific permit from the director/designee. Permit applications must be submitted at least 60 days in advance (waivable in extenuating circumstances) for staff review and SEPA compliance.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Build a 60-day lead time into project scheduling for any job requiring flight on or launched from Washington State Parks land — this is not a same-week approval process, so identify park-sited work early in the proposal stage.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Submit the permit application with enough buffer to absorb SEPA review delays, and retain the approved permit in the project file; do not rely on the 'extenuating circumstances' waiver as a planning assumption.

source_title: Use of aircraft/unmanned aircraft to pursue, concentrate, or harass wildlife; hunting-day restriction
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to pursue/concentrate/harass wildlife; spotting/locating wildlife by drone for hunting purposes; hunting on the same day a UAS was operated
summary: It is unlawful to use a vehicle, aircraft, unmanned aircraft, or motor-propelled boat to pursue, concentrate, or harass wild animals/birds, except as authorized by WDFW for wildlife-conflict purposes. Separately unlawful to use aircraft (including UAS) to spot/locate/report wildlife location for hunting purposes, and to hunt game animals/birds/migratory birds on the same day one has operated a UAS.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Avoid low-altitude pursuit-like maneuvers near wildlife concentrations on environmental-monitoring and corridor-mapping flights — steady, predictable flight paths at planned survey altitude are unlikely to implicate this rule, but circling or diving near animals could.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: If the work is actually part of an agency-directed wildlife-conflict response, contact the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife before mobilization and ask for the applicable authorization and operating conditions. Ordinary environmental monitoring or mapping does not become authorized wildlife pursuit or harassment merely because it serves a professional purpose, so retain the agency direction and mission limits.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document flight altitude and purpose for any survey work near known wildlife concentrations; the hunting-day restriction is not directly relevant to commercial survey operations but is worth a one-line mention in field-crew orientation for staff who also hunt recreationally in Washington.
verification_status: Verified directly against current WAC rule text
notes: Newly identified in this research pass.

source_type: Repealed, expired, or superseded authority (never enacted)

summary: Many third-party drone-law aggregator sites assert Washington has a codified requirement that drones be labeled with owner name/phone number and that operators must obtain landowner consent before overflying private property, often mis-citing 'RCW 47.68.380.' Verified directly: RCW 47.68.380 is actually titled 'Aerial search and rescue — Liability — Definition' and is unrelated. The labeling/consent language originates from House Bill 1049 (2017-18), which stalled in committee and was never enacted.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Don't build a labeling or per-overflight-consent step into Washington field procedures based on this claim — it isn't required by state law. Rely on the actual applicable rules (registration, park rules, privacy statute) instead.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Correct this specific point if it appears in any client-facing compliance document or internal training material sourced from a drone-law aggregator site; citing a nonexistent statute undermines the credibility of the whole compliance package.
